_readme: One entry per project. Order here is the order on the site. To add a project, copy one entry, change the values, and commit. See ADD-A-PROJECT.md.

projects.title: Warehouse
projects.summary: Stock is never stored as a figure. It is derived from an append-only movement ledger.
cardPoints: **Sixteen assertions**, each rule removed once to prove the tests catch it
projects.lede: A Postgres schema for consignment and third-party warehouse stock where stock is never stored as a figure. It is recomputed from an append-only movement ledger, so it has nowhere to drift to.

problem.title: Two sources of truth
problem.text: A stored stock figure has two sources of truth the moment anything goes wrong: the figure, and the transactions behind it. When they disagree there is no way to tell which is right, and adjusting the figure destroys the only evidence.

approach.title: Nothing to disagree with
approach.text: Stock is a view, the sum of movements per barcode and location. A correction is a contra row that points at the row it corrects. The ledger refuses updates and deletes.

result.title: Every balance has a trail
result.text: Every figure traces back to the rows that produced it. A count's variance is an output, never written back automatically, because a count that has seen the expected figure proves nothing.

rows: A trigger that refuses update and delete
Every row records who and when
Not null plus a non-blank check, now() default
A correction is a contra row, never an edit
A check: a correction must point at the row it corrects
It is a view, and a test asserts no such column exists
Delivered quantity per order is computed
A view over issued delivery notes; no column accepts it
A delivery note cannot be issued empty
A trigger on the transition to issued
A count cannot be signed off unowned
A check requiring who counted it

details.title: Mutation pass.
details.text: After the tests run, the script removes each rule from the schema in turn and requires the tests to go red. A test that cannot fail adds confidence without adding evidence.

projects.note: Clean-room version of the data model from a real consignment operation. None of it is anyone's operational data.

projects.title: PO line
projects.summary: Reads barcode and quantity out of partner purchase-order lines, and refuses rather than guesses.
cardPoints: Born from a nine-line order stored as **1, 2, 3 up to 9 pcs**
projects.lede: Reads barcode and quantity out of partner purchase-order lines, and refuses rather than guesses. Every trap it handles cost a real reconciliation before it was understood.

meta.label: Input
meta.value: Text lines from any PDF or sheet

meta.label: Output
meta.value: Read lines, and refused lines with a reason

numbers.label: traps that each produced a plausible wrong number
mutation cases, each must turn the tests red

problem.title: Plausible and wrong
problem.text: Each trap produced a number that looked entirely reasonable on screen. Nothing looked broken until the goods were counted at the counter.

approach.title: One question, answered strictly
approach.text: Take an array of text lines, whatever produced them, and answer one question: which barcodes were ordered, and how many of each. Anything it cannot read with confidence is listed as rejected, with the reason.

result.title: The tests got fixed too
result.text: On the first mutation run two tests stayed green with the parser deliberately broken, which meant they proved nothing. The tests were the thing that got fixed.

items.title: A phone number is twelve digits. So is a barcode.
items.text: Match on length and every letterhead becomes a phantom order line.
items.fix: Compute the EAN check digit. Known internal codes still pass.

items.title: The quantity is not the last small number
items.text: Take the last small number and a box number at the end of the line wins, silently.
items.fix: Read the number standing in front of the unit: EA, PCS, CTN.

items.title: A quantity written "6." with a trailing dot
items.text: The dot pushed the quantity out, and the row index was left. A nine-line order was stored as 1, 2, 3 up to 9 pcs.
items.fix: Drop a trailing dot. A dot inside a number stays a thousands separator.

items.title: A PDF table that is not row by row
items.text: One export gives nine barcodes, then nine descriptions, then nine quantities.
items.fix: Pair by order only when the counts match exactly. Otherwise refuse.

projects.note: Barcodes and lines on this page are illustrative. A tidy table where everything is off by one is more dangerous than a document that admits it could not be read.

projects.title: Inventory
projects.summary: A min/max plan for a five-SKU distributor that scored 100, then an audit of what the plan does to the warehouse.
cardPoints: Audit: **109 days** over warehouse capacity, **87.6%** fill rate
projects.lede: A min/max replenishment plan for a five-SKU distributor, built in Excel for the DQLab x UjiKompetensi hackathon, then audited against its own output. The plan is arithmetically correct and still overflows the warehouse.

numbers.label: final score, on the third submission
unit fill rate the plan delivers
days the plan needs more space than exists

problem.title: When, how much, and will it fit
problem.text: The brief: reorder each SKU when stock drops below its min and order back up to its max. Min and max both come from 6-day demand windows, supplier lead time is 3 days, and warehouse capacity is reported but not allowed to block an order.

approach.title: A daily ledger, not a list of events
approach.text: A reorder today changes stock in three days, which changes tomorrow's reorder. Written naively that is a circular reference. Laid out as one row per SKU per day, 1,825 rows, every arrival reads the order placed 15 rows above, so the whole year resolves in one pass with no macros. The policy was modelled in Python first, and every computed cell was checked against it before submitting.

result.title: Full marks, and three problems the grade does not show
result.text: Read as an operator, the same output shows 38 of 168 order lines arriving at an empty shelf, a warehouse above 100% on 109 days with a peak of 122.8% on 8 June, and 5 purchase orders placed while the previous order for the same SKU was still on its way.

projects.detailAccent: and what they do to the building

items.title: No safety stock in the trigger
items.text: The order is only placed after stock has fallen below min, and it lands three days later. Stock goes negative on 113 SKU-days across the year.
items.fix: Reorder point = lead-time demand plus a buffer sized to a service level

items.title: Five maxes that do not fit together
items.text: Each max was set from its own SKU's demand. Refilled together they need more than the whole warehouse on 109 days, peaking at 122.8%.
items.fix: Smaller, more frequent orders before any talk of more space

items.title: Orders that ignore what is on the way
items.text: The trigger looks at stock on hand only, so 5 orders were placed while an earlier order for the same SKU was still in transit.
items.fix: Trigger on on hand + on order, one extra term

details.title: The first submission scored 17.54.
details.text: Two tasks scored exactly zero: the only two whose cells were entirely formulas. The grader read stored values, and a file written by a script stores formulas with no results. Recalculated, it scored 97.39. The 2.61 points left were 15 cells of 345 that I had rewritten in rows the brief said not to touch. Restored, it scored 100.

projects.note: PT DQLab Distributor Sehari-hari is a fictional company from the brief, and the dataset belongs to DQLab and UjiKompetensi. The fill rate, capacity and duplicate-order findings are my own reading of the output and were not part of the grade. The workbook is not published.

projects.title: Retail
projects.summary: Which SKUs are rising and which ones sell together.
projects.lede: Which SKUs are rising, and which ones customers already buy together, from 42,446 retail transactions. Built in Python for the DQLab x UjiKompetensi hackathon Retail Crisis and Recovery.

problem.title: What to push, what to pair
problem.text: A retailer wants to know which products are gaining, and which products customers already buy together.

approach.title: Two passes over the same data
approach.text: Rising stars first: daily sales value per product, smoothed with a 3-day moving average, keeping only products whose average rose for at least 12 days in a row. Then Apriori over receipts to find products bought together, keeping only rules with a lift of 2 or more that include a rising star.

result.title: A short list to act on
result.text: 13 rising-star SKUs to give space to, and 20 bundling rules to build offers from.

items.title: Rising stars
items.text: A product qualifies when its 3-day moving average of daily sales value goes up for 12 or more days in a row. Growth is measured from the first non-zero average in that streak to its end, and the list is ranked by it.
items.fix: Keep in stock and give shelf space first

items.title: Bundles
items.text: Receipts become one row each, products become yes or no columns. Apriori keeps itemsets in at least 1% of receipts, and a rule survives when the pair appears together at least twice as often as chance (lift 2 or more) and touches a rising star.
items.fix: Bundle offers and neighbouring shelf slots

rows: Daily sales are noisy; a short average shows direction without hiding it
Rising for two weeks is a trend, rising for three days is a promotion
Pairs rarer than that are not worth a shelf decision
Bought together at least twice as often as chance

details.title: Why only bundles with a rising star
details.text: A rule between two flat products is true but not useful this month. Tying the bundle to a product that is already growing gives the offer something to ride on.

projects.note: Hackathon dataset provided by DQLab. The code is kept private out of respect for the hackathon; the method is described in full here.

projects.title: Sales order
projects.summary: Finding sales orders that do not fit their own branch of the business, in one SQL query.
cardPoints: **20 anomalies (3.9%)** in 509 orders, beyond 3 standard deviations
projects.lede: Finding sales orders whose value does not fit their own branch of the business, written as a single SQL query for a DQLab hackathon.
projects.visualCaption: order value per branch · outliers flagged

problem.title: Unusual compared with what?
problem.text: An order value that is normal in one branch of the business can be extreme in another. One threshold for the whole dataset flags the big branches for being big and lets real outliers in small ones slip through. And each order is attached to a node somewhere in a tree up to five levels deep, not to its branch directly.

approach.title: Find the branch, then judge the order against it
approach.text: Each order climbs the node tree, parent by parent, until it reaches the node that sits directly under the root: that is its branch. Average and population standard deviation are computed per branch, and an order is flagged when it sits more than 3 standard deviations from its branch average, in either direction.

result.title: A review list, not an accusation
result.text: 20 orders, 3.9% of the total, each with its branch, distance from the average and z-score, plus a count per branch on top. One query, no temporary tables, as the brief required.

items.title: Walk the tree
items.text: Five self-joins on the node table climb from an order's node toward the root. The first ancestor whose parent is ROOT is the branch.
items.fix: No recursive queries in MySQL 5.7, so the depth is spelled out

items.title: Judge within the branch
items.text: Average and standard deviation per branch. Flag anything beyond 3 standard deviations on either side.
items.fix: Unusual where it happened, not unusual overall

items.title: Summary and detail together
items.text: A UNION ALL returns the count of anomalies per branch and every flagged order with its z-score, in one result set sorted by branch.
items.fix: The brief asked for a single query

details.text:
-- the flag, per branch
WHERE t.nilai_order > s.average + 3 * s.stdev
   OR t.nilai_order < s.average - 3 * s.stdev

-- reported with each flagged order
(t.nilai_order - s.average) / s.stdev AS z_score

projects.note: Hackathon dataset provided by DQLab (Discovering Sales Performance Root Cause Analysis, June 2026). Only the filter is shown; the full query stays private out of respect for the hackathon.

projects.title: LPG distribution
projects.summary: Demand against fulfilment, return rate and delivery speed for a 3 kg LPG sub-agent in West Sumatra.
cardPoints: Delivery from about **1.5 days** in Area A to **3.1 days** in Area C
projects.lede: Demand against fulfilment, return rate and delivery speed for a Pertamina-authorized 3 kg LPG sub-agent in Tanah Datar, West Sumatra.

problem.title: Uneven, leaky, competitive
problem.text: Demand was uneven across three coverage areas, some cylinders came back leaking or defective, and neighbouring agents competed on delivery speed.

approach.title: Five analyses
approach.text: Demand against fulfilment, demand variance per area with the coefficient of variation, return rate against a 0.5% per cycle benchmark, delivery speed per area, and the top and bottom retailers.

result.title: Where to spend the effort
result.text: Delivery took about 1.5 days in Area A and 3.1 days in Area C. The charts point allocation and reorder planning at the areas that need it.

projects.note: Dataset simulated from my own experience as distribution and operations staff at the sub-agent. Figures follow realistic operating parameters, not real records.

projects.title: LPG demand
projects.summary: Which simple method forecasts monthly demand per area best, to time allocation and reorders.
cardPoints: SMA-3, WMA-3 and exponential smoothing compared on **MAE and MAPE**
projects.lede: Which simple method forecasts monthly LPG demand per area best, so allocation and reorders can be timed.

problem.title: Allocation is a forecast
problem.text: Every monthly allocation is a guess about next month. A better guess means fewer empty shelves and less stock sitting in the wrong area.

approach.title: Simple methods, scored honestly
approach.text: Three methods any operator can explain, run per area and scored on mean absolute error and mean absolute percentage error.

result.title: A method per area
result.text: The most accurate method for each area, and a three-month projection from June to August 2026 for allocation planning.

rows: The average of the last three months
Alpha 0.4: recent months count more, older months fade

projects.note: Dataset simulated from real operating experience. For portfolio purposes.

projects.title: Customer
projects.summary: Segmenting buyers to prioritise deliveries and catch accounts that are slipping away.
cardPoints: RFM scores, then **K-Means with k = 4** across **250 accounts**
projects.lede: Segmenting 250 distribution accounts by how recently, how often and how much they buy, to prioritise deliveries and catch accounts that are slipping away.

numbers.label: segments, k chosen by elbow and silhouette
score levels for each of R, F and M

problem.title: Not every account is equal
problem.text: With limited trucks and cylinders, treating every account the same means the best ones wait and the fading ones go unnoticed.

approach.title: Score, then cluster
approach.text: Recency, frequency and monetary value per account, scored in quintiles, then K-Means with k = 4, chosen with the elbow method and silhouette score.

result.title: A plan per segment
result.text: Champions, Loyal, At Risk and Lost, each with its own action for delivery priority and account follow-up.

items.title: Champions
items.text: Fastest delivery promise first; loyalty pricing.

items.title: Loyal
items.text: Regular contact; offer larger order packages.

items.title: At risk
items.text: Reach out before they leave; find out why orders dropped.

items.title: Lost
items.text: Check if reactivation is worth it; move quota to active accounts.

projects.note: Dataset simulated from real operating experience. For portfolio purposes.

projects.title: Ops & SCM
projects.summary: The three LPG studies in one Streamlit app, with an adjustable smoothing factor for the forecast.
cardPoints: Four pages: overview, distribution, forecasting, segmentation
projects.lede: The three LPG studies in one Streamlit app, so the analysis can be explored instead of read.

problem.title: Three studies, three files
problem.text: Distribution, forecasting and segmentation each lived in their own script and charts.

approach.title: One app with controls
approach.text: A filter by area, a smoothing slider for the forecast, an area picker, and a segment filter on the account table.

result.title: Ask it, do not read it
result.text: The best forecasting method is picked by MAPE for whatever area is selected, and each segment comes with its recommended action.

rows: Accounts, monthly volume, fulfilment rate and the return benchmark at a glance
Filter by area; demand against fulfilment, return rate, delivery time
Move the smoothing factor from 0.1 to 0.9, pick an area, see the best method
Segment sizes, frequency against volume, actions, and the account list per segment

projects.note: Data is simulated inside the app from realistic operating parameters.

projects.title: Finance analytics
projects.summary: Sector performance on the Indonesia Stock Exchange and an LQ45 portfolio optimiser.
projects.lede: Sector performance on the Indonesia Stock Exchange from 2022 to 2024, and a mean-variance optimiser over a universe of LQ45 stocks.

problem.title: Return is half the story
problem.text: A sector or a portfolio that returns more is only better if the risk taken to get there is worth it.

approach.title: Markowitz, made interactive
approach.text: Annual returns, a return heatmap and a risk-return scatter by sector. Then portfolio weights optimised for the highest Sharpe ratio and for the lowest variance.

result.title: Adjustable, not fixed
result.text: The number of simulations and the risk-free rate are sliders, so the frontier can be redrawn under different assumptions.

items.title: Max Sharpe
items.text: The weights with the most return per unit of risk above the risk-free rate.

items.title: Min variance
items.text: The weights with the lowest volatility the universe allows.

projects.note: Simulated data based on realistic assumptions, for education and portfolio purposes. Not financial advice.
